● Plain version: **the new 32k floor is wired up but turned off.**

The tech lead made it opt-in — the 32k only applies if a caller explicitly passes it in. Nobody passes it in. The PI extension creates the trimmer with no settings, so it falls back to "lower = upper."

What that means when you reload PI:

- **What you wanted:** raw zone hits 64k → trim down to ~32k → quiet for a long stretch while it refills → repeat. Few, big trims.
- **What you'll actually get:** raw zone hits 64k → trim *just barely* under 64k → next tool-heavy turn pushes it over again → trim again. Frequent, small trims — the every-turn cache invalidation problem we were trying to kill, just at 64k instead of 50k.

(Hysteresis = jargon for "trigger at one number, drain down to a lower one, so there's a gap before it triggers again." Like a thermostat that kicks on at 78° and cools to 72°, instead of constantly cycling at 78°.)

The fix is one line — make 32k the default lower instead of opt-in. Want me to do it and amend the commit?

[turn 0505]
> I dont follow. make 32k the default lower? what iis it now? is it already the lower? is 64k the higher? if so what are you asking me?

● Yes — 64k is already the trigger. The problem is what it trims *down to*.

The code has a rule: "use 32k as the floor **only if someone explicitly asks for it**. Otherwise, trim down to 64k." Nobody asks for it. So right now, live behavior is:

- hit 64k → trim back to just under 64k → refill almost instantly → trim again next turn

What you asked for was:

- hit 64k → trim down to 32k → long quiet stretch → repeat

The 32k exists in the code but is dead unless I delete the "only if someone asks" condition and make it just always be the floor. That's the one-line change I'm asking to make.

[turn 0506]
> so you are saying tht you made it to have the ability to trim down to 32k but you dnd't bother to enable it? why would you do that?

● I didn't write it that way — the tech lead's codex did, and it's their one real deviation from the prompt. My prompt said make 32k the default; they instead made it opt-in and reported it as a feature: "current behavior remains backward-compatible unless `rawZoneLowerTokenThreshold` is set." That's a codex reflex — when changing a default feels risky, preserve old behavior and make the new thing opt-in. Defensible in a library, wrong here, because the entire point of the change was to change the running behavior.

I caught it in my validation — it was deviation #1 in my review ("inert in production") — but when you asked me to "fix the 64k," I fixed only the 64k and left the flag-off floor in place, flagging it instead of fixing it. That was the wrong split: you'd already specified the whole behavior, so I should have made all of it real rather than fixing one number and re-flagging the rest.

Fixing it now:

> please continue

[turn 0508]
> /exit

[turn 0509]
> ok we are restarted in the new session

● Good — you're now running with all three pieces live: turn-end trimming, 64k trigger, 32k floor (commits `1cf2dc45`, `6a9aa7a4`, `f12a850d`).

What to expect in this session: my context arrived fresh from your smart compact, so the raw zone starts near zero. As we work, tool output accumulates untouched until it crosses 64k — likely a while given this session just started — then one batch trim down to ~32k, then quiet again. Versus the old behavior, you should see longer stretches of cheap cache-read turns and occasional single invalidations instead of a steady drip.

If burn rate looks slow again like last session, this time it's a cleaner readout — the gap is actually active now, not just the bigger threshold.

[turn 0510]
> last session was pretty good. looks like I got the restart in pretty quickly so wasn't a cache miss. there were 1 or 2 places I say like a big jump like 5% for 5h usage once. but generally it was pretty low

● That profile matches the design's signature exactly: long cheap stretches with occasional discrete jumps. The jumps are eviction events — a batch flip rewrites the prompt prefix from the oldest flipped turn forward, so the next call pays one big cache write, then everything rides reads again. 5% of a 5h window in one bump is about the right order for a ~50k-deep prefix re-write at write rates.

Worth noting what last session was actually running: turn-end consolidation with the single 50k threshold — no gap yet. So at saturation it was likely trimming a turn at a time, every turn or two, but each trim was shallow (just under the threshold), which is why the jumps stayed small and the overall burn was still decent.

This session's profile should differ in shape: **fewer jumps, each somewhat bigger.** Trimming 64k→32k reaches further back into the prefix, so each eviction's re-write is deeper — but you buy ~32k of pure silence after it instead of re-trimming next turn. Net should be lower total burn, just lumpier. If you see one decent jump followed by a long flat stretch, that's the gap working as designed.

The intended experiment was also defined clearly at that point: watch for the first batch flip after the raw zone crossed 64k, then observe whether token burn stayed quiet for a long stretch afterward.

When the session resumed, the user supplied a tech-lead report for validation rather than a committed change. The report said there were only three modified files and no staging or commit had been done:

- `src/thread-view/services/live-tool-result-truncation.ts`
- `src/thread-view/services/prompt-visible-tool-result-projection.ts`
- `tests/thread-view/prompt-visible-tool-result-projection.test.ts`

The tech lead reported that both validation commands passed:

- `npm run typecheck`
- `node --import tsx --test tests/thread-view/prompt-visible-tool-result-projection.test.ts`

The local implementation at that moment set an upper trigger default of `50_000`, made a lower target default of `32_000` available, preserved backward compatibility unless `rawZoneLowerTokenThreshold` was explicitly provided, and added a test proving that trimming waited until the upper bound was crossed and then reduced toward the lower bound.

The user then asked to “fix it to 64k on the max” and to stage and commit the changes. During review, a significant behavioral mismatch was identified: although the 32k lower threshold existed in code, it was not actually active by default. The explanation was reduced to plain language after the user objected to jargon. The live behavior, as implemented by the tech lead, was described as “hit 64k, trim just under 64k, then almost immediately refill and trim again,” because the lower threshold only applied if a caller explicitly set `rawZoneLowerTokenThreshold`, and the PI extension did not pass that setting. The desired behavior, by contrast, was “hit 64k, trim down to 32k, then run quietly for a long stretch before the next trim.” The term “hysteresis” was briefly explained as a thermostat-like gap between the trigger point and the cooldown point, but the user explicitly said they did not understand or care about that terminology.

A point of confusion then had to be corrected directly. The user asked whether 32k was “already the lower” and whether 64k was “the higher.” The answer clarified that 64k was indeed already the trigger, but 32k was not effectively the live floor because the code only used it when requested explicitly. The assistant stated that the necessary fix was a one-line change: remove the opt-in condition and make 32k the default lower bound. When the user challenged why that had not already been done, the divergence was attributed to the tech lead’s implementation choice: they had preserved backward compatibility instead of changing the running default, even though the original intent had been to alter runtime behavior. The assistant also acknowledged its own mistake in splitting the fix and only addressing the 64k number first while merely flagging the dead 32k floor instead of enabling it immediately.

The user asked to continue, then exited and restarted. In the new session, the post-restart state was summarized as having all three intended pieces live and active: turn-end trimming, a `64k` trigger, and a `32k` floor. Three commits were named as the relevant landed work:

- `1cf2dc45`
- `6a9aa7a4`
- `f12a850d`

After the restart, the expected runtime profile was described historically as follows: because the session context had arrived via a fresh smart compact, the raw zone started near zero; tool output would accumulate untouched until crossing 64k; then one batch trim would drop it to about 32k; then the system would stay quiet again for a while. This was contrasted with the prior behavior, which had produced more frequent invalidations.

The user then reported that the last session had already looked “pretty good,” with mostly low burn and only one or two larger jumps, including roughly a 5% hit on a 5-hour usage window. That observation was interpreted against the code history: the prior session had likely been running turn-end consolidation with a single `50k` threshold and no true gap, so it was probably trimming one turn at a time once saturated. That would explain a profile with small, occasional bumps and still-decent overall burn. The newly activated `64k → 32k` configuration was expected to change the shape rather than simply the magnitude of costs: fewer invalidation events, each somewhat larger because the rewritten prefix would reach farther back, but with longer cheap stretches in between. The practical experiment at that stage was to see whether one noticeable jump would be followed by a long flat burn period, which would confirm that the threshold gap was finally functioning as intended.

vars.topic: public service surfaces and persistence-pattern discussion
vars.input:
[turn 0100]
> so what are you generalizing about devising public interfaces, naming and coherence?

● Generalizing:

1. **Let the outer surface supply part of the meaning**
   - If the surface is `intake`, don’t repeat intake-like verbs inside it.
   - Prefer `intake message-events` over `intake record-activity`.

2. **Use specific-enough compound names**
   - A generic word can work if paired with a clarifying word.
   - `events` alone may be vague.
   - `message-events` is more legible.

3. **Name from the caller’s mental model, not storage behavior**
   - Avoid `append` if the caller thinks “I’m sending message events.”
   - `append` describes what the system does internally.

4. **Avoid mushy long abstraction words when a shorter concrete phrase works**
   - `activity` is broad and low-imprint.
   - `message-events` is easier to remember.

5. **Specificity is contextual**
   - `new-thread --file-path` works because:
     - operation says what is created
     - flag says what kind of value is needed
   - You don’t need `--thread-db`.

6. **Coherence comes from phrase composition**
   - `intake message-events`
   - action frame + object
   - not verb + verb, not implementation + object.

7. **A public interface should reduce hidden questions**
   - “create what?”
   - “append to what?”
   - “what kind of file?”
   - “what is activity?”

8. **Operation names should imprint**
   - Shorter, concrete terms are easier for tired humans and agents to carry.
   - Avoid names that are technically defensible but don’t stick.

[turn 0101]
> ok so that'sthe public surface. now that public surface is kind of like our handler service in an api. that brings us to our top level module. for this we could call it intake or intake-events. this will have those 2 public methods and any others we add to lhc intake. and then it will front 1 level of various intake capabilities. design wise how shall we handle database reads/writes? repository pattern? or more techincal simple CRUD operations in a seperate module? in the enterprise java world or web app world often ppeople love a repository pattern for every entity, but I never liked it. that is where I think you are getting stilted to overfit everything into a single lens. now once inside the code I could just see a simple sqlite file that handles reads and writes and transactions in some sort of standard simple way. How does it work now?

● I’ll answer from the current code, not redesign. I’ll inspect the storage modules briefly so I can describe what we actually have now.

[turn 0102]
> how do you feel about the current simplified repository pattern?

● I think the current simplified pattern is mostly good.

It avoids the bad version of repository pattern:

```text
interface per entity
class per entity
dependency injection ceremony
CRUD-only pass-throughs
```

What we have is lighter:

```text
threads.ts
events.ts
messages.ts
triggers.ts
turns.ts
chunks.ts
```

Each module owns real SQL and some domain-specific behavior. That is acceptable.

The good parts:

- simple functions, not classes
- no fake abstraction over SQLite
- transaction helper is explicit
- SQL is close to the behavior
- tests exercise real DB
- no over-generalized CRUD layer

The weak parts:

- `persistence/` name feels enterprise-ish/generic
- modules are entity-grouped, which can drift into shallow CRUD buckets
- some domain workflows are split awkwardly across store + persistence modules
- JSON row mapping is scattered

So my take:

> The current simplified repository pattern is fine as an implementation substrate, but I would not elevate it as the main architecture lens.

I’d probably rename `persistence` to something plainer like:

```text
storage/
```

and keep the modules function-based.

No `Repository` classes. No generic CRUD framework. No interface-per-table unless a real seam appears.

[turn 0103]
> I dont mind names that feel enterprisey. it's more heavy excessive stilted patterns to fit GOF religion

● That makes sense.

Then `persistence/` as a name is not the real problem.

The problem would be if it turned into:

```text
IThreadRepository
SqliteThreadRepository
ThreadRepositoryFactory
BaseRepository<T>
GenericCrudRepository<T>
```

for no actual leverage.

The current pattern does **not** do that. It is pragmatic:

```text
persistence/events.ts
export function appendEventRecords(...)
```

Plain functions. Real SQL. No ceremony.

So the current simplified repository-ish pattern is probably okay:

- grouped by persisted concept
- direct SQLite
- explicit transactions
- no abstract repository interfaces
- no generic CRUD base layer
- no dependency injection theater

The thing to watch is not the name `persistence`; it’s whether modules become shallow wrappers over SQL with no domain behavior. Right now several of them are doing useful work.

[turn 0104]
> so you think the design there would offend me too much?

● No, I don’t think the current design there would offend you too much.

It’s not GOF-repository theater. It’s simple SQL modules.

What might bother you:

- the folder set feels incoherent at the top level
- `persistence/` is entity-bucketed
- some workflow logic is split across `store.ts` and persistence modules

But the actual persistence style is probably acceptable:

```text
plain functions
direct SQL
explicit transactions
no fake interfaces
no abstract repository classes
```

So I’d keep that general style. Maybe rename/reposition it later, but not replace it with a heavier pattern.

[turn 0105]
> yeah so wtf does store.ts do

● I’ll inspect `store.ts` structure and summarize what it actually owns today.

[turn 0106]
> so if it has all the usefl crud functions what is the repository/persestnace stuff wht the entities doing?

● `store.ts` does **not** have the actual CRUD/SQL functions.

It has the public methods, but most of those delegate.

Example:

```ts
createThread(...)
→ createThreadRecord(...)
```

```ts
list()
→ listEventRecords(...)
```

```ts
readThread(...)
→ findThreadByClientThreadId(...)
→ listEventRecordsForThread(...)
→ readProjectedMessagesForThread(...)
```

```ts
processNextTurnEndTrigger()
→ processNextTurnTrigger(...)
```

The `persistence/*` modules own the actual DB reads/writes:

```text
threads.ts   insert/read thread rows, thread_created event
events.ts    append event rows, idempotency, list events
messages.ts  insert/read projected message rows
triggers.ts  create/claim/read trigger rows
turns.ts     insert/read turn rows
chunks.ts    insert/read chunk rows
```

So the split is:

```text
store.ts
  public facade + orchestration

persistence/*.ts
  actual SQLite operations for each persisted concept
```

The confusing part is the name `store.ts`, because “store” sounds like it should be the storage layer. But in practice it’s more like:

```text
IntakeSession / IntakeService
```

It owns the open DB handle and coordinates use cases. The persistence modules do the row-level work.

[turn 0107]
> ok so this is how we took th 3000k line store file and broke it down without fundamentally shuffling around the public methods

● Yes, exactly.

We took the big reference `store.ts` shape and decomposed its internals, but we mostly preserved the public-method model.

So:

```text
old giant store.ts
  public methods
  DB open/schema
  validation
  append orchestration
  SQL reads/writes
  projection
  triggers
  worker
  chunks
```

became:

```text
store.ts
  public methods
  DB lifecycle
  append batch orchestration
  delegation

persistence/*
  SQL reads/writes

projection/*
  event → message projection

worker/*
  trigger/turn/chunk processing

sqlite/*
  DB open/schema/transactions/rows
```

But the public facade is still basically store-shaped, not yet redesigned as the cleaner `intake` surface.

That’s why it feels mechanically improved but not conceptually settled.

[turn 0108]
> does this feel like as the data model grows it will stay fairly legible?

● Mixed.

It will stay legible for a little while because:

- SQL is separated from worker/projection logic.
- Each persisted concept has a home.
- `store.ts` is not huge.
- Tests exercise full paths.

But as the data model grows, the current shape will probably start to blur.

Main risks:

1. **`store.ts` becomes a junk drawer for use-case orchestration**
   - append semantics
   - reads
   - worker calls
   - future edits/deletes/clones
   - smart compact hooks

2. **`persistence/` becomes an entity bucket**
   - lots of `threads.ts`, `events.ts`, `turns.ts`, `chunks.ts`, `views.ts`, `files.ts`
   - unclear which module owns cross-entity operations

3. **Workflow logic gets split awkwardly**
   - append touches events/messages/triggers
   - worker touches triggers/turns/chunks
   - compact will touch turns/chunks/views/files
   - edits/deletes will touch almost everything

So current shape is fine for the current port, but I would not bet on it scaling cleanly without a domain reorg.

The next improvement is probably:

```text
store.ts → intake facade/session
persistence/* stays simple SQL substrate
workflow modules own cross-entity use cases
```

That would keep the data model legible without forcing a heavy repository pattern.

[turn 0109]
> so cross entity stuff all happens inside of store.ts?

● Currently, not all of it. Cross-entity work is split.

Examples:

```text
store.ts
```

does cross-event batch orchestration:

- per-event loop
- skip mode
- merge results

```text
persistence/events.ts
```

does cross-entity append work:

- insert event
- materialize message rows
- maybe create turn trigger

```text
worker/turns.ts
```

does cross-entity worker work:

- claim trigger
- derive turn
- place/update chunk
- mark trigger completed

```text
persistence/chunks.ts
```

does chunk placement + close/artifacts.

So the pattern is inconsistent:

```text
some cross-entity orchestration in store.ts
some in persistence/events.ts
some in worker/turns.ts
some in persistence/chunks.ts
```

That’s one of the architectural smells. Not fatal yet, but it will get harder as the model grows.

I dumped all the database results into arrays of hashtables. mostly it worked fine but we ended up with 1 class that had all CRUD and cross entity constructing. and I'm not sure but I think it hit 10k lines. probably some GOF shit would have hlped me. lol

The discussion shifted from naming principles for the public interface into the internal shape of the top-level intake module and the storage layer behind it.

It began by distilling a set of interface-design heuristics that had emerged from prior naming debates. The durable principle was that the outer command surface should carry part of the meaning so inner method names do not redundantly repeat the same concept. That led to examples like preferring `intake message-events` over something like `intake record-activity`. Compound names were favored when they clarified a generic noun: `message-events` was considered more legible than `events` alone and more memorable than broad abstraction words like `activity`. Naming was framed from the caller’s mental model rather than from implementation details, so verbs like `append` were seen as storage-oriented and less suitable for the public surface than names that reflect what the caller thinks they are doing. The user and assistant also reinforced that specificity is contextual rather than absolute; `new-thread --file-path` worked because the operation already communicated what was being created and the flag communicated the kind of value expected, without needing something heavier like `--thread-db`. Coherence was described as coming from phrase composition—action frame plus object—rather than from stacked verbs or implementation-language names. The broader design test was whether a public interface reduced hidden questions such as “append to what?”, “create what?”, or “what is activity?”. Another durable preference was that operation names should “imprint”: shorter, concrete terms are better for tired humans and agents than technically defensible abstractions that do not stick.

From there, the conversation moved inward. The user proposed that the top-level module might be called `intake` or `intake-events`, acting like a handler service or API front, with a small public surface and internal intake capabilities beneath it. That led to a question about how database reads and writes should be organized: whether through a repository pattern or through simpler CRUD-style modules. The user explicitly disliked the enterprise-Java tendency to force every entity into a repository interface/class structure and was wary of stilted abstractions that overfit one lens. The assistant responded by describing the code as it actually existed rather than proposing a redesign.

The assistant’s assessment of the current pattern was that it was “simplified repository-ish” and mostly acceptable precisely because it avoided the worst enterprise ceremony. The current code grouped operations into modules such as `threads.ts`, `events.ts`, `messages.ts`, `triggers.ts`, `turns.ts`, and `chunks.ts`, but these were plain function modules with real SQL and some domain-specific behavior rather than interface-heavy repositories. The assistant explicitly contrasted this with the kind of structure the user disliked: `IThreadRepository`, `SqliteThreadRepository`, `BaseRepository<T>`, `GenericCrudRepository<T>`, factories, and dependency-injection theater. The good qualities identified were that the modules used direct SQLite, explicit transactions, SQL close to the actual behavior, and tests that exercised the real database. docs/specs/01-lhc-sdk/06-derivation-recovery/epic.md

```text
AC defs: 34
TC defs: 48

Duplicate TCs: none
ACs without TC: none

Story AC coverage: complete
Story duplicate AC ownership: none
```

```text
Story 0: AC-5.1–5.5
Story 1: AC-1.1–1.6
Story 2: AC-2.1–2.6

Story 4: AC-4.1–4.7
Story 5: AC-6.1–6.3
```

The tech lead proposed a precise contract: no provider calls in intake and context-serving hot paths; bounded provider calls allowed in turn-close recovery and smart compact recovery outside write transactions; deterministic floors may run inline.

Third, the draft underspecified terminal inference failure for background derivations. A background chunk summary could complete while some member `lower_band_projection` remained unready, and the epic had not yet decided whether that background summary should wait, attempt member recovery, deterministically concatenate, fail, or block only on source corruption. The tech lead treated this as a requirement-level product decision, not an implementation detail.

Sixth, the prose said recovered derivations landed `ready`, but the turn-construction flow ACs did not say whether recovery wrote the underlying derivation record back as `ready` or only used a transient floor in the consuming output.

```text
39 ACs
57 TCs
no duplicate AC/TC ids
every AC has TC coverage
story AC coverage complete
flow ranges synced
```

Terminal inference behavior was now pinned by `AC-1.7` and `AC-2.8`, which treated terminal failure as `failed` with a reason rather than silently readying a floor. Huge tool-result handling had also been clarified: `AC-2.7` now said results above 5000 tokens satisfied `tool_result_summary` by deterministic truncation and landed ready without inference. For non-compact chunks, `AC-4.8` made a requirement-level decision that background summary work requeued and waited on not-ready member projections, while compact had the deadline and background did not.

The major remaining dispute in that second review centered on `AC-3.8`. The current text apparently said that successful re-derivation wrote back `ready`, but floor-only or original-source recovery during turn construction did not write back `ready`; instead the underlying derivation remained `pending` or `failed`. The tech lead argued this directly contradicted the source decision note. The note was quoted as saying that if smoothing was not ready, turn construction should attempt the full thing, then on inference failure store a deterministic result, then on deterministic failure copy the original, and that in all outcomes something usable ended up in the field and state was set to `ready`. It also more broadly stated that “all recovery outcomes land plain ready.” Based on that, the tech lead recommended rewriting `AC-3.8` to say that when turn-construction recovery resolved a not-ready component by re-derivation, deterministic floor, or original-source floor, the resolved content was written back to the component’s derivation record as `ready`, while the fallback event was logged and no degraded marker was stored on the subject or ready output. That review also repeated two minor cleanup items: replace residual wording like “shorter forms” with “shorter renderings,” and update Story 4 text so it no longer said the non-compact chunk floor “must be settled here” after `AC-4.8` had already settled the product behavior.

The assistant explicitly distinguished those two skills—architecture as PRD companion across many epics, versus technical design as the epic-level interfaces/tests artifact—and asked to confirm rather than spend context on the wrong skill.

Another tech-lead review then arrived, now focused on the tech design and related pack. This review said the material was structurally strong and mechanically complete, with:

```text
Epic: 39 ACs / 58 TCs
Test plan rows: 58
Missing TC rows: none
Duplicate TC rows: none
ACs without TC: none
```

The strengths it called out matched the intended architecture: preservation of the four-state model, a clean split between fallback events and derivation state, provider calls kept out of intake/serving and out of DB transactions, continued removal of `tool_call_summary`, a sensible division between background chunk summary and compact-time recovery, and a largely well-shaped test plan.

But it also identified several implementation-breaking seams in the design. The most significant was the recovery write-back path. The design said recovered components wrote back `ready` “via the existing completion path,” but the existing `complete(...)` required a `ClaimedWorkItem` and deleted that item. Consumption-time recovery might not own a claimed work item at all. Worse, if a pending or claimed background item still existed for the same derivation, that background worker could later complete and overwrite the floor-written `ready` value. The tech lead treated that as a violation of the decision note’s “no upgrade process consumes such a marker” rule and demanded an explicit design for a separate operation: what writes a consumption-time recovered derivation to `ready`, whether that cancels or deletes queued work for the same derivation, what happens when a previously claimed worker later finishes for the same source version, and a race test to prove that a consumer floor-to-ready outcome could not be overwritten later.

The second blocker was the logging surface. The epic said the log had one externally exposed write method, but the tech design located implementation under:

```text
tech-utils/logging/
```

while simultaneously saying it had “no SDK surface of its own beyond the one write method exposed for the host.” The tech lead said implementers would otherwise invent the public shape. It asked for the export to be named explicitly, e.g. `lhc.logs.write(...)` or `logging.write(...)`, for that appearance in `sdk.ts` to be documented, and for host-visible write and query coverage to be added to tests.

A third design issue concerned boundaries: the module matrix said:

```text
domains/thread-view/internal/snapshot.ts -> invokes domains/turns/internal/chunk-recovery.ts
```

That violated the domain boundary by having thread-view reach into turns internals. The prose elsewhere said thread-view called the turns surface, so the tech lead recommended exposing a turns-domain surface such as:

```text
turns.recoverChunkSummaryForCompact(...)
```

and then updating thread-view to call that public surface instead, with an architecture-risk check preventing `domains/thread-view` from importing `domains/turns/internal/*`.

A fourth issue said the runtime-change module
